lessons.title: Resolution is three knobs, not one slogan
explanation: The smallest half-pitch a tool can print is not 'the wavelength'. It is the Rayleigh relation: CD ≈ k1 · λ / NA. Three symbols. λ is the wavelength of the light. NA is the numerical aperture of the projection optic — how wide a cone of rays it can collect. k1 is a dimensionless process factor that packs resist, illumination, and later tricks into one number. Shrink CD by shrinking λ, raising NA, or lowering k1. There is no fourth magic word on this slide.

Directionality is the lesson. Cut λ in half and, other terms fixed, you can print about twice as tight. Raise NA and the same thing happens. Lower k1 and you are spending process cleverness, not buying a new lamp. The industry rode λ for decades (365 → 248 → 193 nm), then spent NA and k1 because the next wavelength was late. 'Smaller light, smaller transistors' is the λ term with the other two erased.

A working number: 193 nm light, NA 0.93, k1 of 0.31 gives CD ≈ 0.31 × 193 / 0.93 ≈ 64 nm. That is a half-pitch scale, not a marketing node. Change one knob, the number moves. The twenty-minute unit will add the cost: raising NA also thins the slice of height that stays in focus.
lessons.example: Two otherwise identical 193 nm processes: one at NA 0.75, one at NA 0.93, same k1. The second prints a tighter pitch. A third process that keeps NA 0.75 and pretends k1 can fall to 0.15 without changing illumination or resist will miss CD — the equation is not a slogan you shout at the wafer.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every later DUV trick and the EUV jump is a sentence about these three knobs. If you cannot name them, '3 nm' will look like a length.

lessons.title: The same knobs spend depth of focus
explanation: The ten-minute unit named CD ≈ k1 · λ / NA. This one is the bill. Depth of focus — the slice of height where the image stays sharp — shrinks as roughly λ / NA². Raise NA to buy resolution and you spend the focus budget as the square. Cut λ and you buy both a tighter pitch and, other things equal, a thinner slice. There is no knob that only helps.

That is why the last course treated CMP as a lithography input. A 200 nm local step next to a 150 nm depth of focus is not a 'rough wafer'. It is two planes, and the lens has one. Dose cannot invent a second slice. The incoming flatness is part of the Rayleigh story even though it does not appear in the CD equation.

Work a pair of numbers. 193 nm at NA 0.93 has CD ≈ 0.31 × 193 / 0.93 ≈ 64 nm and a depth of focus on the order of 193 / 0.93² ≈ 220 nm. Push NA to 1.35 (the immersion unit will say how) and CD drops to about 44 nm while depth of focus falls toward 193 / 1.35² ≈ 110 nm. You bought pitch. You spent height.
k1 is the remaining escape hatch, and it is not free either — the next unit. For now: any briefing that names a tighter pitch and never names depth of focus has shown you one half of Rayleigh.
lessons.example: A metal layer moves from NA 0.93 to a higher-NA recipe to hit pitch. The same incoming 80 nm of leftover topography that used to sit inside the focus slice now straddles it. One side of each die prints; the other side's CD walks. The wavelength did not change. The slice got thinner than the hill.
lessons.whyItMatters: High-NA, later, is this same trade at a new wavelength. If you learn it here as physics, the later platform is a number. If you skip it, High-NA will look like a product name.

lessons.title: k1 is cleverness packed into a number
explanation: k1 is the leftover in CD = k1 · λ / NA after you have named the lamp and the lens. It is not a material. It is a score for how much of the theoretical resolution your process actually uses. Off-axis illumination, a contrasty resist, optical proximity correction, and later multipatterning all push k1 down. A naive, on-axis, uncorrected process sits at a high k1 and wastes the optic you paid for.

There is a floor. Imaging theory will not let k1 fall much below about 0.25 for a single exposure — you cannot pass spatial frequencies the optic does not collect. Pushing from 0.40 toward 0.30 is real process work. Pretending k1 is 0.15 on a single 193 nm exposure is pretending the equation has a fourth knob. That is usually when someone invents a second exposure instead.

So shrinking k1 is not a free substitute for a shorter wavelength. It spends illumination complexity, mask complexity, and process window. A briefing that says 'we improved k1' and never names what got harder has hidden the bill. Wavelength and NA are hardware. k1 is everything else you did to the image.
lessons.example: A 193 nm, NA 0.93 layer at k1 = 0.40 prints about 83 nm. The same hardware at k1 = 0.30 prints about 62 nm — because the team paid in off-axis illumination and OPC, not because λ changed. Asking the same tool for k1 = 0.18 as a single exposure is how a multipatterning program starts.
lessons.whyItMatters: DUV 'tricks' later in this course are k1 programs with names. If k1 is a mystery coefficient, immersion and OPC will look like folklore.

lessons.title: The legal band of focus and dose
explanation: A feature has a legal critical dimension — a CD spec. The process window is the set of focus values and dose values that still land inside that spec. It is a region on a plot, not a vibe. Outside the region, the line is too thin, the hole is scummed, or the wall has fallen over. Inside, the stencil is legal enough to transfer.

Focus and dose trade. A little extra dose can sometimes hold CD when focus walks, and a little extra focus latitude can forgive a dose miss — until they cannot. The window shrinks as you ask Rayleigh for more: smaller k1, higher NA, thinner depth of focus. A process that 'prints' at one sweet-spot field and dies at the edge of the die is a window problem, not a mystery defect.

You already know both axes. Dose is the number you can miss both ways. Focus is the slice Rayleigh just priced. The window is those two, together, against a CD bar. The next unit is how a lab measures that region — a focus-exposure matrix, read as a Bossung plot.
lessons.example: A gate CD spec is 48 ± 2 nm. At best focus the legal dose band is 28–34 mJ/cm². Walk 80 nm out of focus and the band collapses to a point, then vanishes. Dies at the wafer edge, where the chuck is a little high, fail CD even though the scanner 'used the same recipe'.
lessons.whyItMatters: Yield lectures that say 'process window' without a focus axis and a dose axis are using a slogan. This is the object those lectures owe you.

quiz.correctAnswer: The focus and dose ranges that still print a legal CD

lessons.title: The Bossung plot is a lab object
explanation: A focus-exposure matrix (FEM) is how you measure the window instead of asserting it. You print a grid: columns of focus, rows of dose, or the other way around. Each site gets a CD measurement. The plot of CD versus focus at several doses is a Bossung plot. It is not a brand. It is a family of curves that smile or frown as you walk through focus.

Read it like a map. A dose whose curve stays inside the CD spec across a wide focus range is a wide window. A dose whose curve only kisses the spec at one focus is a point, not a process. The isofocal dose is the one whose CD barely moves with focus — often the dose you want, if it also sits in spec. When every curve is a steep V, you do not have a window. You have a prayer.

The FEM is also how you catch a lie. A scanner recipe that 'always prints' may print at the FEM center and die at ±50 nm of focus, which is a real chuck and a real wafer bow. The process-window unit named the region. This unit is the experiment that draws it.
lessons.example: A metal FEM shows 30 mJ/cm² staying inside 64 ± 3 nm from −60 to +60 nm of focus. 24 mJ/cm² is legal only at best focus. The team picks 30, not because it is a lucky integer, but because the Bossung curve is the flatter one inside spec.
lessons.whyItMatters: Without this plot, 'we have a process window' is a sentence anyone can say. With it, you can point at a curve and a spec bar.

quiz.correctAnswer: A printed grid of focus and dose that maps the process window

lessons.title: The wall is not a straight line
explanation: A drawn line is a pair of perfectly straight edges. The developed resist wall is not. Line-edge roughness (LER) is the wiggle of that wall along its length. Line-width roughness is the same wiggle read as a changing CD. Both come from a film that is molecular, a develop that is statistical, and an image whose edge is a gradient, not a cliff.

On a wide line the wiggle is a cosmetic. On a 40 nm line the same nanometres of wiggle are the CD. A locally thin spot becomes a fuse. A locally wide spot eats the space to the neighbor. After etch, the roughness often transfers into the hard film, so the device sees it, not just the stencil.

You do not need EUV photon counting yet to own this. Any resist edge is rough. Dose, bake, and developer can move the number; they cannot draw a Euclidean line. The later stochastics unit is what happens when the photon count itself is a small integer. This unit is the wall you already have at DUV.
lessons.example: Two gates drawn at the same CD: one with 2 nm LER, one with 6 nm. The second population has a fat tail of locally thin gates that fail voltage. The mean CD on the metrology bar was in spec. The wall was not a line.
lessons.whyItMatters: CD is an average. Devices die on the local minimum. If the wall is 'the drawing', you will not understand a spec that names roughness.
